title: Satan
summary: The adversary, devil and accuser identified in Scripture, whose power remains subject to God's authority.

claims.text: Job 1:6-12 presents Satan questioning the motives of a righteous man in the heavenly assembly. God permits a limited test but does not grant unrestricted authority. The Hebrew title in this passage is explained as the adversary or accuser in the ESV translation note.

Revelation 12:9-10 explicitly identifies the dragon as the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, and depicts the accuser being cast down. These are connected designations within that particular vision.
In the temptation narrative, Jesus rejects the devil's demands and answers from Scripture. The Gospel account presents the tempter as an opponent, not a rival deity.
Revelation's account of Satan's final punishment precludes treating him as an independent sovereign of hell. His actions and judgement are described in relation to divine authority.

Scripture provides descriptions of conduct and symbolic imagery rather than an exhaustive physical portrait, fixed rank within a later occult hierarchy or complete chronology of origin. The traditional identification of Lucifer with Satan requires separate study of Isaiah 14 and is not assumed here.

title: Beelzebul (Beelzebub)
summary: A designation used in accusations against Jesus, with a debated relationship to the god of Ekron and to Satan.

claims.text: Matthew records the Pharisees attributing Jesus' exorcisms to Beelzebub. Mark attributes a similar charge to scribes from Jerusalem, and Luke records an accusation by some of those present. The King James Version uses Beelzebub while the NIV uses Beelzebul.
In answering the accusation, Jesus argues that Satan cannot sustain a kingdom divided against itself. He attributes his works to God's power and connects their accomplishment with the kingdom of God.
Second Kings describes Ahaziah seeking an answer about his injuries from Baalzebub, identified in the narrative as the deity of Ekron. Elijah condemns the king's turning away from the God of Israel.

Jesus' answer connects the Beelzebul accusation with Satan's kingdom. This supports interpreting the designation in relation to Satan, but the passage does not provide a separately named biography or establish a second-in-command within a demonic hierarchy.

The similarity between the name in Second Kings and its New Testament forms warrants linguistic and historical research. The Biblical texts do not explicitly establish the precise etymological development or whether every historical use refers to one individual being.

title: Legion
summary: The collective designation of many demons in the Gospel accounts of the man restored by Jesus near the Sea of Galilee.

claims.text: Mark describes a man living among tombs, whom Jesus encounters after crossing the sea. In the narrative, the response to Jesus' question about the spirit's name identifies a plurality of beings under the designation Legion.
Luke's parallel account explains the designation by reference to the many demons that had entered the man. The spirits petition Jesus not to send them into the deep.
The narratives describe Jesus permitting the spirits to enter a herd of pigs, followed by the herd's destruction. Mark reports a herd of approximately two thousand animals.

The number of animals is not a stated count of the demons. Legion functions here as a collective designation; the texts do not give names, ranks or numbers for individual members or identify a commander.
The account concludes with the man restored, clothed and sitting in his right mind. Jesus directs him to return to his people and tell them what God has done for him.
The dignity and restoration of the afflicted man are central to the narratives. This ancient account does not provide a diagnostic method for contemporary mental or physical distress.

title: Abaddon (Apollyon)
summary: The angel of the abyss named in Revelation 9:11, whose designation and role must be read within the fifth trumpet vision.

claims.text: Revelation 9 introduces a fallen star given a key to the abyss. Smoke emerges and visionary locusts are released. Their power is expressly limited in its duration and its permitted effects.

Revelation 9:11 names the angel of the abyss as king over the locusts. It supplies the Hebrew name Abaddon and the Greek name Apollyon for the same figure; the ESV footnote glosses the names as destruction and destroyer respectively.
Job 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11 use the Hebrew term Abaddon in expressions concerning destruction or the realm of the dead. The KJV renders it as destruction, while the ESV preserves the term Abaddon.

The Old Testament uses do not automatically identify a personal angel in those passages. Revelation applies the designation to a figure in a particular apocalyptic vision; its literary context therefore matters.

The text explicitly describes kingship over the visionary locusts. It does not say that Abaddon rules every demon, is Satan, or occupies a fixed rank in a universal spiritual hierarchy. Whether the fallen star of verse 1 and the angel of verse 11 should be identified is not explicitly resolved.

title: Azazel
summary: The disputed designation in Leviticus 16 and the rebellious figure called Azazel in the Book of Enoch.

claims.text: Leviticus 16:7-10 describes two goats presented before the Lord. One is designated for the Lord and the other for Azazel in the ESV; the KJV uses scapegoat. The second animal is sent into the wilderness alive.
The subsequent passage associates the sending away of the live goat with the removal of Israel's iniquities. The rite belongs to the Day of Atonement and is directed by God's instructions to Aaron.

The ESV footnote acknowledges uncertainty over the meaning of Azazel, including a place or a demonic being as possibilities, alongside the traditional rendering scapegoat. Leviticus alone does not establish a personal biography, angelic rank or independent cult.

In 1 Enoch 9-10, Azazel is named in connection with wrongdoing and receives a sentence of confinement. The Enochic narrative presents a personal figure in a way that Leviticus does not explicitly develop.
The Enochic account should not be used to resolve the disputed Levitical term by assumption. The two texts need to be examined independently before proposing a historical or theological relationship.

title: Belial (Beliar)
summary: A term associated with wickedness in the Old Testament and contrasted with Christ in Paul's correspondence.

claims.text: In Deuteronomy 13:13 and 1 Samuel 2:12, the KJV uses expressions involving Belial for wicked people. The ESV renders the relevant descriptions in terms of worthlessness rather than a named spiritual being.

In 2 Corinthians 6:14-16, Paul places Belial in contrast with Christ amid a sequence of contrasts involving righteousness, darkness, faith and idolatry. The NIV footnote identifies Beliar as a Greek variant of Belial.
The contrast in Paul's letter supports an understanding of Belial as a designation of opposition to Christ, rather than establishing that every Old Testament occurrence refers to a named demon.

The New Testament passage does not supply a separate genealogy, physical appearance, territorial assignment or rank for Belial. Identification with Satan is an interpretative question and is not a separately established entity biography.

title: The prince of Persia
summary: The opposing prince described in Daniel 10, considered within the angelic conflict of the vision.

claims.text: Daniel 10:13 records the heavenly messenger's explanation that the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted him for twenty-one days, until Michael, described as one of the chief princes, came to assist him.
The messenger later speaks of returning to fight the prince of Persia, of the coming prince of Greece, and of Michael as Daniel's people's prince.

The visionary context and Michael's involvement strongly support a spiritual interpretation of the opposing prince. Nevertheless, the passage supplies a title rather than a personal name, and the term prince is not intrinsically a demonic rank.
Daniel 10 does not provide a universal map of territorial spirits, a method of identifying modern national demons or a mandate to diagnose geopolitical events as demonic activity.
The narrative emphasises God's answer to Daniel and the revelation of events concerning his people. It should not be reduced to speculative charts of the unseen realm.

title: Semjaza
summary: The leader named in the Enochic account of the Watchers' descent, distinguished from figures explicitly named in Scripture.

claims.text: First Enoch 6 presents Semjaza as the leader of heavenly beings who desire human wives. He fears bearing the consequences alone; the others agree to share responsibility. The narrative locates their descent at Mount Hermon and describes a company of two hundred.

First Enoch 10 places the judgement of Semjaza and his associates in a divine commission to Michael. The text describes confinement following the death of their children and anticipates final judgement.
Within this account, Semjaza's leadership concerns the particular group of Watchers. It does not establish leadership over all rebellious angels, the devil, or every evil spirit.
Genesis 6 and Jude 6 do not name Semjaza. The name and individual role in this profile are attested in ancient literature, not established by those Biblical passages.

title: The prince of Greece
summary: The second opposing prince mentioned in Daniel 10 and the limits of identifying spiritual counterparts to earthly kingdoms.

claims.text: At the end of Daniel 10, the heavenly messenger announces renewed conflict with the prince of Persia and the coming of the prince of Greece (Grecia in the KJV). The following verse names Michael as Daniel's people's prince.

The parallel with Persia's prince and the messenger's earlier description of heavenly assistance support a spiritual reading of the figure. The passage does not identify a personal name, rank beyond the title, or an exact relationship with a historical ruler.

The announcement belongs to Daniel's prophetic setting. It does not establish that a corresponding spirit governs modern Greece or provide a method of identifying spirits assigned to contemporary nations.
The princes of Persia and Greece should be indexed as separate designations because Daniel mentions them separately. Their relationship to a wider hierarchy remains unspecified.

title: Asmodeus
summary: The demon named in Tobit, studied within the book's narrative and its differing canonical reception.

claims.text: Tobit 3 identifies Asmodeus as the cause of the deaths of Sarah's seven husbands. The narrative distinguishes this attribution from the unjust accusation made against Sarah and presents her appeal to God in distress.
In the narrative, God hears both Tobit's and Sarah's prayers and sends Raphael to help them. The account of the demon's flight and restraint in chapter 8 forms part of that divine response.

The Catholic Church explicitly includes Tobit in its canon, and the Orthodox Church in America identifies it as part of the longer Old Testament canon. Protestant editions generally distinguish such books from their Old Testament canon.

The source is therefore identified as deuterocanonical Scripture, not treated as a universally accepted addition to the archive's shared Biblical corpus. The account concerns a particular named demon; it does not establish a universal rank or a domain over a class of human behaviour.
The story emphasises divine providence and prayer. Its particular narrative actions should not be extracted as an instruction for contemporary diagnosis, treatment or exorcism.

title: Armaros
summary: A named Watcher in the Book of Enoch, examined through the text's limited attributed role.

claims.text: The leaders listed in 1 Enoch 6 include Armaros. The narrative identifies the group as leaders of the company of heavenly beings that descends in the days of Jared.
First Enoch 8 attributes to Armaros knowledge associated with undoing enchantments. This is an attributed role in the text, not a verified ability or an endorsement of the practice.
The passage provides neither a detailed biography nor an independent rank beyond the group leadership described earlier. Later claims about the figure require separate documentary evidence.
Genesis 6 does not identify Armaros. The name is recorded as part of the Enochic narrative rather than as an explicit Biblical designation.

title: Baraqijal
summary: A Watcher named in Enochic literature and associated there with knowledge of astrology.

claims.text: Baraqijal is named among the leaders in 1 Enoch 6:7. The Charles translation subsequently associates the name with astrology in chapter 8.

The text presents the attributed teaching within its larger account of corruption and judgement. It does not establish the supernatural effectiveness of astrology, nor does it provide a detailed biography of the named figure.

The Biblical record of the sons of God in Genesis 6 does not supply this name or attributed teaching. A reader should distinguish the narrative's named leaders from the less specific Biblical testimony.
This profile uses the spelling of the Charles edition. Comparison of alternative manuscript spellings and etymologies remains a separate philological task.

title: Spiritual warfare in Ephesians 6
summary: The passage describes spiritual struggle and directs believers towards God's strength and armour.

claims.text: Ephesians 6:12 distinguishes the struggle against spiritual powers from conflict against flesh and blood. The surrounding passage directs believers towards God's strength, faith, righteousness, salvation, Scripture and prayer.

The text does not supply a named demonic hierarchy or a technique for diagnosing spiritual causes in other people. Its practical emphasis is faithful resistance rather than speculation about particular entities.

title: The authority of Jesus Christ over demons
summary: The Gospel of Mark presents Jesus' authority over unclean spirits as part of the revelation of his identity and teaching.

claims.text: In the Capernaum synagogue, an unclean spirit recognises Jesus. Jesus commands it to be silent and to leave the man; the narrative describes its departure and the onlookers' astonishment.

The narrative places the emphasis on Jesus' authority, not on an independent power held by the spirit or an elaborate ritual. The recognition of Jesus by an evil spirit does not constitute faithful discipleship.
This account cannot establish that modern symptoms of distress have the same cause. It should not be used as a diagnostic checklist.

title: The nature and origin of demons
summary: What Scripture establishes about demons and rebellious angels, and what it leaves unresolved.

claims.text: Mark and Luke describe a man afflicted by many demons, using the language of unclean spirits and devils in the same account. The narratives present these as personal spiritual agents subject to Christ's authority.

Matthew 25:41 associates the devil with his angels. Second Peter and Jude describe angels who sinned or abandoned their appointed habitation and are held for judgement. These passages establish rebellion and accountability but do not identify every unclean spirit as one of those imprisoned angels.

The identification of demons with fallen angels is a theological synthesis rather than an explicit universal definition in these passages. Their exact origin, the relationship between active demons and imprisoned angels, and a detailed chronology of rebellion remain unresolved by these texts.

A responsible Biblical account begins with the authority of God over spiritual evil. Speculation about the composition of the unseen realm must not obscure the central narrative of Christ restoring the afflicted man.

title: Angelic rebellion and judgement
summary: The Biblical testimony concerning angels who sinned and their accountability before God.

claims.text: Second Peter invokes the judgement of sinful angels as a precedent for divine judgement. Jude describes angels who abandoned their appointed place and are kept for the day of judgement.

Jesus' discourse on final judgement identifies everlasting fire as prepared for the devil and his angels. The passage places these spiritual beings under divine judgement, rather than portraying them as independent rulers of a rival eternal kingdom.

The two epistles describe sinful angels in comparable terms, but neither passage expressly identifies them with every demon in the Gospel narratives. A complete chronology or identification with the sons of God in Genesis 6 requires separate contextual analysis.

title: The Nephilim: Genesis and Numbers
summary: A study of the two Biblical passages that name the Nephilim, distinguishing the narrative from later claims about their origins.

claims.text: Genesis 6:1-4 places the Nephilim in the period associated with the sons of God and the daughters of men. The King James Version renders the term as giants. The passage also refers to mighty men of old and men of renown.
Numbers 13 records the spies' report concerning the inhabitants of Canaan. In verse 33 the spies connect the giants with the sons of Anak and describe their own apparent smallness.

The report in Numbers belongs to the fearful response of the spies, not to an independent description of the exact height or ancestry of these inhabitants. The narrative distinguishes Caleb's confidence from the other spies' discouraging report.

Genesis 6 does not explicitly call the Nephilim demons or state that their spirits become demons after death. Numerical estimates, descriptions of supernatural powers and a precise account of their ancestry cannot be established from these passages alone.

The interpretation of the sons of God is relevant but should be investigated separately from the identification of the Nephilim. Later traditions may explain the relationship in greater detail, but those explanations require their own sources and evidence classifications.

title: Principalities, powers and spiritual authorities
summary: Paul's descriptions of spiritual powers within the wider Biblical teaching of Christ's supremacy.

claims.text: Ephesians 6 contrasts the believer's struggle against spiritual forces with warfare against flesh and blood. Its list includes principalities, powers, rulers of darkness and spiritual wickedness.

Ephesians 1 places the risen Christ above every principality and power, might and dominion. Colossians 1 states that all things, visible and invisible, including thrones and authorities, were created through and for Christ.

Because the terminology also occurs in statements concerning creation and Christ's supremacy, the words principality and power cannot be treated as universally demonic titles without considering the context of each passage.

Colossians 2 presents Christ's triumph over powers in connection with forgiveness and the cross. A Christian study should give this victory priority over constructing speculative chains of demonic command.
The lists do not supply names, territorial assignments or a complete hierarchy. The texts establish spiritual opposition and Christ's supremacy, not a comprehensive taxonomy of ranks.

title: Unclean spirits in the Gospel narratives
summary: The Gospel accounts' terminology, the plurality of spirits and Christ's restoration of the afflicted.

claims.text: Mark 5 refers to an unclean spirit and then to multiple spirits speaking through the afflicted man. Luke's parallel explicitly explains the designation Legion by reference to the many demons that had entered him.

The term Legion is a collective designation in these narratives. Although Mark records a herd of about two thousand pigs, the text does not establish the exact number of spirits or a named commander in an organised demonic hierarchy.

The restoration of the afflicted man, and his subsequent testimony about what God had done for him, are central to both accounts. The narratives do not warrant diagnosing present-day distress as possession on the basis of similar symptoms.

title: Spiritual deception and false teaching
summary: Biblical warnings about false apostles, misleading appearances and teachings that depart from the faith.

claims.text: Paul warns the Corinthians against deceptive workers presenting themselves as apostles of Christ. He compares their conduct with Satan's appearance as an angel of light. The immediate context concerns false claims to apostolic authority.

First Timothy warns that some will abandon the faith through deceptive spiritual influence and false teachings. The passage gives specific examples and contrasts them with gratitude for God's creation.

A religious appearance is therefore not sufficient evidence of divine authority. The Christian evaluation of a teaching requires attention to its message and conformity with Scripture, rather than the impressiveness of its messenger.

These warnings do not establish that every mistaken teaching has a demonstrable supernatural origin. The text's theological claims should not be converted into accusations about named contemporary individuals without evidence.

title: The final judgement of Satan and evil
summary: Revelation's account of Satan's defeat, final judgement and the limits of chronological speculation.

claims.text: Revelation 20 depicts Satan being released, deceiving the nations and gathering them against the saints. Their assault ends with divine judgement, and the devil is consigned to the lake of fire.
The subsequent vision describes judgement before the great white throne, the opening of books and the defeat of death and hell. The lake of fire is also identified as the second death.
The narrative does not portray Satan as the sovereign of hell. He is himself subject to punishment. The central emphasis is God's ultimate authority over evil and death.
Christian traditions interpret the chronology and literary symbolism of Revelation differently. The stated judgement is distinguished here from disputed reconstructions of the end times.

title: Christ's victory over the devil and spiritual powers
summary: New Testament teaching places Christ's saving work at the centre of the defeat of evil.

claims.text: Hebrews connects Christ's sharing in human nature and his death with the defeat of the devil and liberation from the fear of death.
First John describes the destruction of the devil's works as a purpose of the Son of God's manifestation.
Colossians places the triumph over principalities and powers alongside forgiveness and the cancellation of the record of debt at the cross.
Taken together, these passages provide a Christ-centred framework for demonology; they do not provide a complete chronology of spiritual rebellion or a comprehensive classification of demonic beings.

title: The sons of God in Genesis 6
summary: The identity of the sons of God in Genesis 6 and the main interpretative questions.

claims.text: Genesis describes the sons of God seeing the daughters of men and taking wives. The passage occurs before the description of widespread wickedness and the flood narrative.

The heavenly-being interpretation draws support from the phrase sons of God in Job, where the narrative depicts a heavenly assembly. Genesis itself does not explicitly name the sons as angels or describe the mechanism of their union.

A human-lineage interpretation reads the passage in relation to the preceding genealogies, particularly the lines of Cain and Seth. Genesis 6 does not explicitly identify the sons with Seth's descendants or the daughters with Cain's descendants.

Another interpretation relates the sons of God to powerful human rulers. The taking of wives and the reference to renowned mighty men are relevant to that reading, but the passage does not explicitly identify the sons as kings.

The heavenly-being reading has a meaningful textual parallel in Job; the competing readings require different contextual inferences. The present entry treats the identification as a disputed interpretation and reserves the treatment of the Watchers in ancient literature for a separately sourced study.

title: Satan in Scripture: adversary and accuser
summary: The Biblical portrayal of Satan as an adversary under God's authority, from Job to Revelation.

claims.text: Job 1 depicts Satan questioning Job's motives before God. The permission granted to test Job includes an explicit limit concerning harm to Job's person.

Revelation 12 identifies the dragon with the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, and describes him as a deceiver and accuser. The vision portrays his defeat and the triumph of the faithful through the Lamb.

The two passages portray opposition to God and accusation of the faithful, while locating the adversary within the limits of divine authority. Neither supplies a complete biography or an exhaustive account of his origin.
Revelation's dragon is presented in an apocalyptic vision. Its imagery should not be treated as evidence of a physical appearance outside that literary setting.

title: Lucifer and Isaiah 14
summary: The morning-star imagery in Isaiah's taunt against Babylon and its traditional interpretation in relation to Satan.

claims.text: Isaiah 14:4 introduces a taunt against the king of Babylon. The following poetic passage describes his downfall and the collapse of his claims to exalted power.
The KJV uses Lucifer in Isaiah 14:12, whereas the NIV uses morning star with the associated dawn imagery. These renderings belong to the same verse.

The New Testament separately depicts Satan's fall in Luke 10:18 and identifies the ancient serpent and dragon with Satan in Revelation 12. It does not explicitly quote Isaiah 14:12 as a personal name for Satan.

A traditional Satanic interpretation reads the ruler's pride and descent as an image of supernatural rebellion. The direct literary referent remains the king of Babylon; any further application requires theological argument.

Lucifer is therefore indexed here as a disputed traditional designation, rather than a separate independently established demon. A chronological narrative of Satan's origin cannot be derived from this passage alone.

title: The Watchers in Daniel and Enoch
summary: A comparative study distinguishing the holy messengers in Daniel from the rebellious Watchers of ancient Enochic literature.

claims.text: Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 4 describes a watcher and holy one who descends from heaven and announces judgement. Verse 17 associates the proclamation of the watchers with the sovereignty of the Most High.
Genesis 6:1-4 describes the sons of God and daughters of men, without naming the sons Watchers or specifying Mount Hermon.
First Enoch 6 describes heavenly beings who agree to descend and take human wives. The Charles translation identifies Semjaza among the leaders and places the descent on Mount Hermon.
First Enoch 9-10 develops a narrative of accusation and judgement involving the rebellious heavenly beings, including Azazel and Semjaza. This account supplies details beyond Genesis.

Daniel's holy watchers should not be identified automatically with the rebellious group in Enoch. The comparison establishes a shared conceptual vocabulary, not identical conduct or a universal angelic classification.
Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 attest sinful angels and judgement. A connection with the Enochic narrative can be investigated, but those verses do not themselves supply its names, numbers or locations.

title: The Enochic account of the origin of evil spirits
summary: A study of 1 Enoch 15-16 as an ancient explanation of evil spirits, compared with the limits of Biblical testimony.

claims.text: First Enoch 15:3-7 contrasts the heavenly Watchers' former spiritual condition with their unions with mortal women. The narrative treats their conduct as a transgression of the boundaries of their appointed existence.

First Enoch 15:8-12 attributes the origin of earthly evil spirits to the offspring of the Watchers and human women. Its account distinguishes these spirits from their heavenly progenitors and depicts them as afflicting earthly inhabitants.
First Enoch 16:1 connects their continued destructive activity with the deaths of the giants and anticipates its termination at final judgement.

This is a distinct ancient origin account, rather than merely another name for the fallen-angel interpretation. The Enochic tradition distinguishes rebellious heavenly beings from the spirits associated with their offspring.

Genesis 6 mentions the Nephilim but does not describe their postmortem spirits becoming demons. The Gospel narratives attest unclean spirits, without supplying this genealogy. The Enochic explanation is therefore recorded as tradition rather than explicit Biblical doctrine.

title: The serpent in Genesis
summary: The temptation narrative in Genesis 3 and the identification of the ancient serpent with Satan in Revelation.

claims.text: Genesis 3 describes the serpent questioning God's command, contradicting the warning of death and presenting disobedience as desirable. The narrative subsequently records human disobedience and God's judgement.
Revelation 12:9 identifies the dragon with the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan. Revelation therefore makes explicit an association that is not stated by the name Satan in Genesis 3 itself.
Reading the passages together supports the Christian identification of Satan with the adversarial serpent imagery. It does not establish a separate demonic individual called the serpent.

The theological emphasis is deception and human disobedience under God's judgement. The texts do not explain the physical mechanism of the serpent's speech or provide a basis for regarding ordinary snakes as demonic beings.

title: Antichrist in the Johannine letters
summary: The Biblical meaning of antichrist, its present manifestations and the distinction between Satan and eschatological opposition to Christ.

claims.text: First John 2:18 speaks both of an anticipated antichrist and of many antichrists already present. Verse 22 associates the designation with denial of Jesus as the Christ and denial of the Father and Son.
First John 4:1-3 places discernment of spirits alongside confession of Jesus Christ's coming in the flesh. Second John 7 identifies deceivers who deny that confession with antichrist.
The Johannine language is not confined to an individual appearing at the end of history. It describes a recognisable form of opposition to Christ already present among the letter's readers.

The designation should not be conflated automatically with Satan himself, Revelation's beasts or the man of lawlessness. These comparisons may inform eschatological interpretation but the passages use distinct terminology.
Doctrinal discernment does not justify identifying particular contemporary figures as the final Antichrist on the basis of political dislike, numerical speculation or unsupported rumours.

title: The beast from the sea
summary: A study of Revelation 13:1-10, including its distinction between the dragon and the beast.

claims.text: Revelation 13 describes a beast rising from the sea, combining features of several animals and receiving authority from the dragon. The text presents the dragon and the recipient of its authority as distinct figures within the vision.
The beast utters blasphemies and makes war on the saints. The vision assigns a limited duration to its authority and calls the saints to endurance and faith.

The imagery invites comparison with the beasts in Daniel 7, but this does not by itself settle the beast's historical, symbolic or future identity. The presence of heads, horns and animal features belongs to the visionary description.
Revelation does not use the Johannine term antichrist for the sea beast. Their identification within an eschatological system must be presented as interpretation, not as an explicit textual equation.

Revelation 19 describes the defeat of the beast and false prophet, while Revelation 20 describes the devil's subsequent judgement. The narrative distinguishes the opponents rather than portraying them as interchangeable names.

title: The beast from the earth and the false prophet
summary: A study of deceptive religious authority in Revelation 13 and the later description of the false prophet.

claims.text: Revelation 13:11-15 introduces a second beast, rising from the earth, with lamb-like horns and a voice likened to a dragon. Its signs direct inhabitants towards worship of the first beast.
The vision associates the second beast's coercive measures with the mark and the first beast's name or number, including restrictions on buying and selling.

Revelation 19:20 recounts the false prophet performing signs on behalf of the beast and deceiving people who received its mark. These shared functions strongly support identifying the false prophet with the second beast, although the comparison is drawn across passages.
Revelation 16:13-14 distinguishes the dragon, beast and false prophet, and separately describes unclean spirits going out from them. It characterises these spirits by deceptive signs.
The apocalyptic figures should not be represented as a catalogue of named demons. The emphasis is deceptive authority and opposition to God, culminating in divine judgement.

title: The man of lawlessness
summary: Paul's description of the adversary in 2 Thessalonians 2, distinguished from Satan and compared with other eschatological texts.

claims.text: Second Thessalonians 2:3-4 describes a figure associated with rebellion, self-exaltation and opposition to what is worshipped. The KJV renders the designation man of sin; the NIV uses man of lawlessness and notes the variant reading.
Verses 8-12 associate the lawless one's appearance with Satan's activity, deceptive signs and the rejection of truth. The Lord's coming brings the adversary's defeat.

Paul's distinction between the figure and the activity of Satan argues against treating these designations as identical in this passage. The figure is opposed to God and dependent on satanic activity, not an equal rival to Christ.

Connections with John's antichrist language and Revelation's beast are important interpretative questions. Paul does not use either designation in this account, and the passage does not supply enough information to identify a contemporary individual conclusively.

title: Michael and spiritual conflict
summary: The Biblical descriptions of Michael's assistance, contention and role in the heavenly conflict.

claims.text: Daniel 10 names Michael among the chief princes and describes his intervention on behalf of the heavenly messenger. Daniel 12 associates him with protection of Daniel's people in a time of distress.

Jude describes Michael as an archangel and reports his contention with the devil concerning Moses' body. Michael invokes the Lord's rebuke rather than pronouncing a condemnatory judgement on his own authority.
In Revelation 12, Michael and his angels oppose the dragon and its angels. The vision identifies the dragon with Satan and depicts the adversary's expulsion.

These passages give Michael specific roles without offering an exhaustive system of angelic ranks. He is a faithful heavenly opponent of evil and must not be classified as a demon in the encyclopaedia.
The account of conflict remains subordinate to God's sovereignty. Revelation's wider explanation locates the victory of the faithful in the Lamb rather than encouraging worship of angels.

title: The temptation of Jesus Christ
summary: A comparative study of the wilderness temptation accounts and Christ's rejection of the adversary's offers.

claims.text: Matthew and Luke describe Jesus fasting and being tempted in the wilderness. The tempter challenges his sonship in connection with physical hunger and proposes a demonstration of divine protection.
Both narratives record an offer of earthly dominion conditional upon worship of the devil. Jesus rejects the demand and affirms that worship belongs to God alone.
The Gospel accounts arrange the temptations differently: Matthew places the temple scene before the offer of kingdoms, while Luke places it afterwards. Both conclude with Jesus resisting the tempter.

The tempter's appeal to Scripture in the temple episode demonstrates that quoting a Biblical passage does not establish the truth of the use made of it. Jesus' response rejects the proposed test of God.
The devil's claim of delegated authority in Luke is a reported assertion within the dialogue. It must not be read in isolation as proof of unlimited sovereignty over creation.
The narratives direct attention to Christ's faithfulness and the rightful worship of God rather than to the tempter's outward appearance or supposed magical powers.

title: False prophets and deceptive signs
summary: Biblical criteria for discernment when religious claims are accompanied by extraordinary signs.

claims.text: Deuteronomy 13 warns Israel against abandoning God even if a sign announced by a prophet comes to pass. The covenant's demand for faithfulness is not made conditional on the success of a sign.
Jesus warns that misleading claimants and false prophets will employ signs to deceive. His warning calls disciples to attentiveness rather than assuming impressive acts prove divine authority.
Second Thessalonians associates the lawless one's appearance with deceptive signs and Satan's activity, while 1 John directs believers to test claims about spirits and their confession of Christ.

Across these passages, the theological content and allegiance of a religious claim matter more than claims of extraordinary power. The comparison does not establish that every alleged miracle is either genuine or demonic.

Modern reports require independent evidence and ordinary explanations must remain open. Claims about spirits must not be used to diagnose an individual or excuse harm against a supposed false prophet.

title: Divination and the spirit of divination
summary: Biblical prohibitions of divination and the account of the exploited woman in Acts 16.

claims.text: Deuteronomy 18:9-14 prohibits divination and related practices within Israel's covenant setting. The passage contrasts seeking such knowledge with faithfulness to the Lord.
Acts 16:16-18 describes an enslaved woman whose fortune-telling brought income to her owners. Paul addresses the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ, and the narrative records its departure.
The owners react to the loss of their income by seizing Paul and Silas. The narrative connects their subsequent imprisonment with that commercial loss and accusations before the magistrates.

The woman's exploitation is significant to the account. It presents a person in need of liberation, not a spiritual technique for readers to imitate. Accurate-sounding religious language does not by itself establish divine authority.
The passage records a specific spiritual attribution. It does not establish that every modern claim of fortune-telling has a supernatural cause, nor does it justify diagnosing individuals.

title: Necromancy and the medium at Endor
summary: The consultation at Endor in 1 Samuel 28, its judgement in Chronicles and the dispute over the apparition.

claims.text: First Samuel 28 places Saul's consultation with the medium at Endor in the context of military fear, Samuel's death and the absence of an answer from the Lord.
The narrative identifies the figure addressed by Saul and the subsequent speaker as Samuel. The message announces judgement and the coming defeat of Saul and Israel.
First Chronicles 10:13-14 connects Saul's death with his unfaithfulness and consultation of a medium, placing the episode within divine judgement.

A reading in which Samuel actually appears follows the narrator's identification. Other interpretations propose deception or a spiritual impersonation. The narrative does not describe the figure as a demon or explicitly explain the mechanism of the appearance.
The event is not presented as permission to consult the dead. The explicit prohibition in Deuteronomy and the judgement in Chronicles are the governing theological context.

title: 1 Enoch: the Book of the Watchers
summary: An introduction to the opening section of Ethiopic Enoch, its account of angelic rebellion and its place in Christian reception.

claims.text: The 1917 English translation by R. H. Charles presents chapters 1-36 as the opening division of 1 Enoch. This entry focuses on the narratives in chapters 6-10 rather than treating every section of the composite work as one continuous account.

Chapters 6-10 describe the descent of heavenly beings, human corruption, the accusation of the transgressors and divine judgement. The narrative includes personal names and locations not given in Genesis 6.

Daniel Assefa's 2022 study documents the canonical standing and historical reception of Enoch within Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity. The study discusses variations among Ethiopian canonical lists and the central role of the Gospels and Pauline writings in the liturgy. Other traditions do not necessarily assign Enoch the same canonical status.

citations.locator: Antiquity; The Ethiopian Canon in the Twentieth and the Twenty-First Centuries

claims.text: This archive distinguishes the historical evidence for the text and its reception from the truth status of the supernatural claims it contains. Its details are not automatically treated as explicit Biblical teaching under the archive's editorial framework.

citations.locator: Antiquity; The Ethiopian Canon in the Twentieth and the Twenty-First Centuries

claims.text: The connection between Enochic traditions and the New Testament deserves separate study. Jude 14-15 attributes a prophetic statement to Enoch; this does not by itself resolve the canonical status of every part of the surviving work.

citations.locator: Antiquity; The Ethiopian Canon in the Twentieth and the Twenty-First Centuries

title: Justin Martyr: the Second Apology
summary: An early Christian account of angelic rebellion and the origin of demons, written in an apologetic context.

claims.text: In chapter 5, Justin explains human wickedness partly through a narrative of angels failing in their appointed responsibilities. He describes their unions with women and identifies their offspring as demons.

Justin applies this account to pagan mythology, arguing that acts attributed to the gods were in fact the work of transgressing angels and their offspring. This serves his defence of Christianity before a non-Christian audience.

The account resembles the Enochic tradition in distinguishing the offending angels from their offspring. Justin's formulation does not explicitly state in chapter 5 that the offspring first die and then become disembodied spirits; the distinction from 1 Enoch 15 must be preserved.

The work establishes that this origin interpretation was expressed by an early Christian apologist. It does not establish a unanimous teaching of the early Church or supply an explicit genealogy of demons in Genesis.

title: Athenagoras: A Plea for the Christians
summary: The early Christian distinction between fallen angels and the wandering souls of the giants.

claims.text: Chapter 24 argues that angels possess freedom of choice and that some abandoned their appointed responsibilities. It describes the giants as the offspring of transgressing heavenly beings and women.

citations.locator: A Plea for the Christians, chs. 24-25

claims.text: Chapter 25 explicitly distinguishes fallen angels from the souls of the giants, which the author identifies as demons. His explanation assigns different origins and motives to the two classes.

citations.locator: A Plea for the Christians, chs. 24-25

claims.text: In chapter 26, Athenagoras connects demonic activity with idolatry. This is part of his argument against accusations of atheism and his defence of Christian worship.

citations.locator: A Plea for the Christians, chs. 15-17, 26

claims.text: Athenagoras provides clear historical evidence that a distinction resembling the Enochic origin account circulated among early Christians. This is evidence of an interpretation, not independent verification of the claimed supernatural genealogy.

citations.locator: A Plea for the Christians, chs. 24-25

title: Tertullian: Apology
summary: A study of Tertullian's attributed origins of demons in the context of his defence of Christians.

claims.text: Chapter 22 discusses angels and demons as spiritual beings and describes a demonic offspring arising from angels who fell through their own choice.
Tertullian also describes Satan as the chief of demons in this chapter. This records the author's terminology, rather than a complete list of ranks or positions.

The argument resembles Justin's account of angelic offspring, while Athenagoras more explicitly identifies the demons as souls of giants. Their distinct formulations should not be compressed into a single quotation or doctrine.

citations.locator: A Plea for the Christians, chs. 24-25

claims.text: These authors provide historical witnesses to early Christian interpretations of spiritual evil. Their writings do not independently establish the supernatural origin of demons, and their assertions must be considered alongside Biblical testimony.
